Background Deficient and insufficient vitamin D status (defined as serum 25(OH)D < 30 nmol/L and > 50 nmol/L) is prevalent worldwide and associated with decreased muscle strength and poor bone health. We aimed to investigate the effect of vitamin D fortification on bone markers and muscle strength among younger adult women at risk of vitamin D deficiency. Methods A 12-week randomised double-blinded placebo-controlled winter intervention trial, providing 30 μg vitamin D 3 /day through fortified yoghurt, cheese, eggs and crisp-bread or similar placebo products. Participants were 143 women of Danish and Pakistani origin 18–50 years of age, living in Denmark, randomised into four groups stratified by ethnicity. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) by LC-MS/MS and the secondary endpoints: four specific bone markers (osteocalcin (OC), Bone specific Alkaline Phosphatase (BALP), Procollagen type 1 amino-terminal propeptide (P1NP), C-terminal crosslinked telopeptide of type 1 collagen (CTX)) and three muscle strength measures (handgrip, knee extension strength, chair-standing), were assessed using one-way ANOVA, Tukey HSD and subsequent linear ANCOVA models, adjusted for relevant covariates. Results Significantly increased serum 25(OH)D concentration from 53.3 (17) to 77.8 (14) nmol/L and from 44.5 (21) to 54.7 (18) nmol/L among Danish and Pakistani women in the fortified groups, respectively ( P < 0.05). The bone turnover markers OC, BALP, P1NP and CTX did not change significantly. Muscle strength by handgrip, knee extension and chair-standing test did not change significantly following the intervention. Conclusions Consumption of vitamin D fortified foods for 12 weeks did not result in significant changes of the bone turnover markers OC, BALP, P1NP and CTX. Muscle strength measured as hand grip strength, knee extension strength and chair-standing did not change significantly following the intervention. Keywords Vitamin D Ranomised controlled trial Immigrants Food Fortified Muscle strength Bone resorption Bone regeneration http://dx.doi.org/10.13039/501100005192 Danmarks Tekniske Universitet http://dx.doi.org/10.13039/100011259 FP7 International Cooperation 613977 Tetens Inge issue-copyright-statement © The Author(s) 2019 Introduction Vitamin D has a well-established role in the calcium and phosphorus homeostasis and is essential for bone health [ 1 , 2 ]. Studies have shown associations between vitamin D deficiency and insufficiency, here and throughout this paper, defined as serum 25(OH)D concentrations < 30 and < 50 nmol/L, respectively [ 3 , 4 ], and non-skeletal endpoints such as muscular atrophy, muscle pain and decreased muscle strength [ 5 – 7 ]. Vitamin D deficiency and insufficiency is a prevalent worldwide problem [ 8 ]. Especially in northerly countries such as Denmark in which the absence of vitamin D from UVB sources during winter increases the risk of deficiency and insufficiency [ 9 , 10 ]. Immigrants (first generation and descendants) living in Denmark as well as other Nordic countries are considered at risk of vitamin D deficiency due to factors such as skin colour, cultural clothing and dietary habits [ 11 – 13 ]. Bone tissue is a dynamic structure that undergoes constant remodelling, and optimal bone health is a balance between bone resorption and bone formation. In a case of chronic bone resorption, the bone mineral density (BMD) will decrease with time [ 14 ]. The bone turnover can be monitored by bone biomarkers in the blood, and is therefore a potential cost-effective method to complement BMD measurements in situations where BMD is not a feasible endpoint e.g. studies of shorter duration [ 14 , 15 ]. Recent advances have located vitamin D receptors (VDR) within muscle tissue, supporting the assumption that vitamin D has an effect on muscle function [ 16 , 17 ]. Some intervention studies have found an effect of vitamin D on muscle strength [ 18 , 19 ] and some effect in the number of falls [ 20 ], while other studies were unable to see an effect [ 21 ]. These inconsistent trends may be related to the baseline serum 25(OH)D concentration and the effect of vitamin D supplementation is more pronounced on vitamin D deficient people (25(OH)D concentrations < 25–30 nmol/L) [ 18 , 19 ]. Additionally, assessment of the effect of vitamin D on muscle strength has primarily been studied among elderly subjects (mainly community dwelling), and there is a lack of data on the effects of vitamin D on muscle strength in young adults deficient in vitamin D [ 22 ]. The mechanism of vitamin D and muscle function has not been agreed upon, however, it has been hypothesised that the active metabolite of vitamin D (1,25(OH) 2 D) vitamin D is involved in the regulation of the calcium flow within the muscle through genomic and non-genomic pathways and is thus important for the contraction of muscle fibres [ 5 , 17 ]. We aimed to investigate the effect of 12 weeks of intervention with vitamin D fortified foods on markers of bone turnover and muscle strength in a population of women of Danish and Pakistani origin between 18 and 50 years of age, at risk of vitamin D deficiency. Our hypothesis was that 12 weeks of intervention with 30 μg vitamin D 3 /day would significantly improve muscle strength in a population of Danish and Pakistani women at risk of vitamin D deficiency.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Vitamin D fortification, vitamin D status, and ethnic differences
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Vitamin D is essential for bone health, playing a well-established role in calcium and phosphorus homeostasis. For muscle function, it is hypothesized that the active metabolite of vitamin D (1,25(OH)2D) regulates calcium flow within muscle via genomic and non-genomic pathways, crucial for muscle fibre contraction. Furthermore, a vitamin D status above 50 nmol/L is suggested to maintain PTH concentration within the normal range, preventing calcium release from bone matrix to support calcium balance.
related_biomarkers: C-terminal crosslinked telopeptide of type 1 collagen (CTX)

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary:
The study was a 12-week randomized controlled trial providing 30 
µg vitamin D3/day through fortified foods (yoghurt, cheese, eggs, crisp-bread) versus similar placebo products. No dose-response findings or comparisons of different fortification levels were conducted within this study. It was noted that a relatively high baseline serum 25(OH)D concentration in the participants (49.6 (18) and 46.9 (22) nmol/L) might have contributed to the lack of effect on bone turnover markers, suggesting a threshold effect for vitamin D supplementation.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The intervention was highly specific, as fortified and non-fortified foods were designed to be identical in fat percentage and nutrient content, with vitamin D3 being the sole differentiator. The study targeted women specifically 'at risk of vitamin D deficiency' based on restrictive inclusion criteria (low fish/supplement intake, low UVB exposure). However, despite this specificity, the intervention did not result in significant changes in the bone turnover markers (OC, BALP, P1NP, CTX) or muscle strength measures (handgrip, knee extension, chair-standing).

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: The target population was 143 younger adult women (18-50 years) of Danish (n=71) and Pakistani (n=72) origin living in Denmark (Copenhagen area, 55°N) who were at risk of vitamin D deficiency. This risk was defined by inclusion criteria such as low consumption of fish/fish products (less than weekly), low intake of vitamin D-containing supplements (less than weekly), no use of tanning facilities, and no planned sun-holiday.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Deficient and insufficient vitamin D status is associated with decreased muscle strength and poor bone health. The intervention successfully increased serum 25(OH)D levels, aiming to effectively and safely improve vitamin D status in both ethnic groups. While a vitamin D status of >= 50 nmol/L is considered sufficient for maintaining healthy muscle and bone, the intervention did not significantly change bone turnover markers or muscle strength in this population. Baseline analysis revealed health disparities, with women of Pakistani origin reporting poorer self-reported health, higher BMI, higher fat percentage, and lower lean mass compared to Danish women.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Vitamin D deficiency and insufficiency are classified as an adverse risk for bone and muscle health, and these conditions are prevalent. The intervention aimed to provide a protective benefit by improving vitamin D status and maintaining muscle and bone health at sufficient vitamin D levels. The study also highlighted adverse health disparities between ethnic groups at baseline. The findings also suggest diagnostic utility for identifying vitamin D deficiency.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The reliability of several biomarkers was assessed, including detailed precision (SD/CV) for Osteocalcin (OC), Bone specific Alkaline Phosphatase (BALP), Procollagen type 1 N-terminal propeptide (P1NP), C-terminal crosslinked telopeptide of type 1 collagen (CTX), Serum 25(OH)D (LC-MS/MS method certified by VDSP with intra-assay CV < 5% and inter-assay CV < 6%), and Serum creatinine. Hand grip strength and Knee extension strength showed high inter-rater and test-retest reliability (intra-assay CVs 4.0% and 4.2% respectively). While bone biomarkers are generally considered cost-effective for monitoring bone turnover in shorter studies, they exhibit large pre-analytical and analytical variability and are influenced by numerous modifiable factors (circadian rhythm, season, ethnicity, fasting, physical activity, menstrual cycle), often lacking standardized assays. Inconsistent trends in vitamin D's effect on muscle strength may be linked to baseline serum 25(OH)D concentrations, with effects more pronounced in severely deficient individuals (< 25-30 nmol/L). The current study may have been underpowered and too short (12 weeks) to detect relevant changes in muscle strength and bone markers.
recommended_alternatives: BMD measurements (as a complement to bone biomarkers, especially in longer studies)
